blocks.note: surface reading: a kindly person who does favours for others
setter's reading: turns as in somersaults and flips, performed well in a circus act

explanation.surface: A description of a helpful, charitable neighbour.
explanation.walkthrough: A good turn is usually a kind deed; here the turns are physical somersaults, done skilfully.
explanation.definitionFit: A circus performer whose act consists of tumbles, flips and somersaults performs physical turns with skill.

clue.text: Girl who is sweet on tarts, perhaps

blocks.note: first meaning: a female given name
second meaning: candied plant stems used to decorate cakes and pastries

explanation.surface: A young woman who is fond of loose women, or of pastries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sweet on' looks like 'fond of', but the sweet is a candied decoration sitting on top of tarts.
explanation.definitionFit: Angelica is a feminine name, and also a herb whose green crystallised stalks decorate cakes and trifles.

blocks.note: p (piano) is the musical marking for soft
Asti is an Italian sparkling wine, here in the plural

explanation.surface: An order at the bar: soft drinks and sparkling wines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drink soft' reads like 'soft drink', but soft is just the musical letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastis is an aniseed-flavoured French aperitif, usually diluted with water before serving.

blocks.note: black is a colour
in cricket the on side is also called the leg side

explanation.surface: Painting a crusty wound some shade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' is not a position word here: in cricket, on and leg name the same half of the field.
explanation.definitionFit: A scab is a worker who refuses to join a strike, and blackleg is the older British term for such a strikebreaker.

clue.text: Exotic Baroda is foreign to me

definitions.note: an adverb of place, 'in foreign parts'

indicators.note: something exotic is strange and unfamiliar, so the following word's letters take on an unusual form

blocks.note: an Indian city, taken as written

explanation.surface: A British traveller finds the Indian city of Baroda strange and unfamiliar.
explanation.walkthrough: Baroda (now Vadodara) is a city in Gujarat; its six letters rearrange exactly.
explanation.definitionFit: Being overseas means being in a country other than your own, one that is foreign to the speaker.

blocks.note: surface reading: the junior pupil in a school class
setter's reading: a form is the shallow nest where a hare lies, so the youngest there is its baby

explanation.surface: Pointing out the baby of a school class.
explanation.walkthrough: A form is a British school class, but also the hollow in grass where a hare rests.
explanation.definitionFit: A leveret is a hare in its first year, the young animal that lies in the hare's grassy hollow.

clue.text: Lads can be involved in dishonour

indicators.note: being involved means being tangled up together, so the letters get mixed through each other

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Young men risk getting caught up in disgrace.
explanation.definitionFit: A scandal is public disgrace or loss of reputation brought about by shameful conduct.

indicators.note: something used is worked over and handled, so these letters have been reworked

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Equipment a shoemaker has been working with.
explanation.definitionFit: Clobber is British slang for one's clothes, belongings or kit, the same sense as gear.

blocks.note: first meaning: a herbal liqueur first made by monks in Normandy
second meaning: following the Rule of St Benedict, as monks do in religious houses

explanation.surface: Someone drinks habitually at a numbered venue.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As a rule' suggests 'usually', but it is literal: the monastic rule written by St Benedict, followed in 24-across.
explanation.definitionFit: Benedictine is a French liqueur, and Benedictine monks live under the monastic Rule of St Benedict.

indicators.note: an intruder is something lodged inside, so the word sits within the phrase that follows

blocks.note: spans the end of the composer's name and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: A disguised theme slipped into the opening of a piece by the French composer Poulenc.
explanation.definitionFit: Covert action is concealed and secret, kept hidden from view as if behind a veil.

clue.text: Kind of order that's never found out

blocks.note: first meaning: a religious community whose members live apart from the world
second meaning: shut in, so never to be found outside

explanation.walkthrough: 'Found out' suggests being caught cheating; here it means literally being found outdoors.
explanation.definitionFit: An enclosed order of nuns or monks stays inside its walls, and anything enclosed is shut in rather than out.

blocks.note: the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer military reserve
a cricket or football side has eleven players, written XI

explanation.surface: Arranging a coach for the second-string side.
explanation.definitionFit: A taxi is a hired car that carries passengers, one form of transport.

clue.text: But it could be handy in a put-up job

definitions.text: But it could be handy in a put-up job

blocks.note: surface reading: a fraud or frame-up arranged in advance
setter's reading: a task of putting something up high, such as hanging curtains

explanation.walkthrough: A put-up job is a rigged scheme, but read literally it is any work done at height.
explanation.definitionFit: A folding set of steps lets you reach high places when fixing shelves or hanging things.

clue.text: Cheap drink! It makes for an expansive habit

definitions.text: It makes for an expansive habit

blocks.note: a farthing was a quarter-penny, the smallest old British coin
ale is a drink

explanation.surface: A bargain pint, which encourages a widening drinking habit.
explanation.walkthrough: Habit means clothing here, not a routine; 'cheap' stands for a coin worth almost nothing.
explanation.definitionFit: A farthingale was a hooped petticoat worn under Tudor skirts to spread them wide, so a broad garment.

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone was forced to make a train come off the rails.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram has no separate signal; 'derail' itself suggests knocking things off course.
explanation.definitionFit: A tailored suit is made to measure, cut and sewn specially to fit the wearer.

blocks.note: first meaning: a small spotted beetle
second meaning: a female bird

explanation.walkthrough: Mother Goose sounds like the nursery-rhyme teller, but she is simply a female of her species.
explanation.definitionFit: The ladybird is a red spotted beetle (ladybug in America), and a mother goose is a female feathered creature.

indicators.note: messing about means jumbling things up, so the letters are put in disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
J is the abbreviation for jack in a card pack

explanation.surface: An order to quit fooling about with a friend called Jack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Messing around' reads as one phrase, but 'around' is the material being messed.
explanation.definitionFit: To adjourn a meeting is to suspend or halt it until a later time.

clue.text: It keeps children occupied with toys

definitions.text: It keeps children occupied with toys

blocks.note: surface reading: something that entertains children
setter's reading: it literally holds young children inside, along with their toys

explanation.walkthrough: 'Occupied' looks like 'busy', but the enclosure is occupied in the sense of filled by the little ones.
explanation.definitionFit: A playpen is a portable fenced enclosure in which a baby or toddler can safely play.

indicators.note: one thing in another means it sits inside it
dodgy means unreliable or crooked, so the word's letters are not straight

blocks.note: the letters of trade rearranged
the Mini is a classic small British car

explanation.surface: A shady second-hand car dealer at work.
explanation.definitionFit: To administer a remedy or punishment is to give it out or dispense it, so to supply.

clue.text: Reserve place in theatre for freezer

blocks.note: ice means reserve or frostiness of manner
a box is a private compartment of seats in a theatre

explanation.surface: Booking seats at a playhouse in an icy auditorium.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Reserve' looks like the verb 'book', but it is the noun for a cool, aloof manner.
explanation.definitionFit: An icebox is a refrigerator, or the compartment within one where food is kept frozen.

blocks.note: first meaning: in fact, truly
second meaning: read as a verb, to form an alliance once more

explanation.walkthrough: The second sense splits the word as RE (again) and ALLY (befriend).
explanation.definitionFit: Really means in truth or in fact; re-ally means to join forces anew after a split.

blocks.note: a do is a party or celebration
L is the abbreviation for line, doubled for the plural

explanation.surface: A political stooge who toes the party line.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Following party lines' suggests obedient politics; it just tells you what the letters come from.
explanation.definitionFit: A doll is a toy figure, and figuratively a person manipulated like a puppet.

indicators.note: most of something is not all of it, so the end of the following word is cut off

blocks.note: taken as written
to own up is to admit

explanation.surface: Even the best stand-ups confess their gigs sometimes flop.
explanation.walkthrough: Only the first five letters of comedians are kept, a generous reading of 'most'.
explanation.definitionFit: A comedown is a decline in status or a letdown after high hopes, an anticlimax.

blocks.note: surface reading: the Houses of Parliament at Westminster
setter's reading: the great church in Westminster, a religious house

explanation.walkthrough: Westminster suggests Parliament's two Houses, but the famous church there is the model.
explanation.definitionFit: Westminster Abbey is a great church, and an abbey is a house of monks or nuns.

clue.text: Soldier, foul-mouthed in simile or trope, perhaps

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the letters are only one possible arrangement of the answer

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A grammar lesson on figures of speech about a coarse-tongued soldier.
explanation.walkthrough: The simile is 'to swear like a trooper'; a trope is a figure of speech, which fits the literary surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A trooper is a private cavalryman or soldier, famously used as the standard of heavy swearing.

indicators.note: something provoked is stirred up, so its letters are agitated into a new order

blocks.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
taken as written

explanation.surface: A cleric was almost goaded into sweet-talking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nearly' looks like it trims a word, but it is the material being stirred.
explanation.definitionFit: Blarney is smooth, charming talk meant to win favour, named after the Irish stone said to give eloquence.
